title: Respiration in Plants
tagline: Respiration as energy release from food, aerobic and anaerobic respiration, the basic respiratory equation, and the evidence from experiments.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Respiration is one of the most important life processes because it is how cells release energy from food. In plants, just as in animals, respiration happens all the time, in every living cell, and it is not the same as breathing. This chapter explains respiration as a breakdown of food with the release of energy, gives the simple equations commonly used in ICSE work, distinguishes aerobic respiration from anaerobic respiration, and shows how experiments can provide evidence that respiration occurs in germinating seeds and other living plant tissues.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Respiration releases energy from food in living cells

facts.label: Two kinds
facts.value: Aerobic respiration (with oxygen) and anaerobic respiration (without oxygen)

facts.label: Common equation
facts.value: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy

blocks.text: Respiration is the process by which living cells break down food substances and release energy for life. It is not the same as the physical movement of air in and out of lungs or other organs; in plants there is no such breathing organ, but every living plant cell respires. Respiration takes place in the cytoplasm and mitochondria of cells and helps the plant grow, absorb materials, transport substances, repair itself and carry out all other life activities. The food most often used in respiration is glucose, and energy is released as the glucose is oxidised. Because energy is needed for every active process, respiration is often called the energy-releasing life process.

items: Respiration is the release of energy from food in living cells.
It occurs in all living plant cells, all the time.
Respiration is not breathing; plants do not 'breathe' in the animal sense.
Glucose is the common food used in respiration.
Aerobic respiration uses oxygen; anaerobic respiration does not.
Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.

items.text: A germinating seed respires actively because it is growing and needs energy.
items.note: Germinating seeds are a standard example of respiration in plant tissues.

items.text: A green leaf respires by day and night, though during the day photosynthesis may produce more oxygen than the leaf uses.
items.note: Respiration and photosynthesis are different processes even when they happen in the same tissue.

blocks.text: Aerobic respiration is respiration in the presence of oxygen. In this process glucose is broken down fully and carbon dioxide and water are produced, with a relatively large amount of energy released. Anaerobic respiration is respiration without oxygen. In this process glucose is only partially broken down, less energy is released, and products such as ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, or sometimes organic acids, are formed depending on the organism. In plants and yeast, anaerobic respiration often produces alcohol and carbon dioxide; in animal muscle cells under oxygen shortage it produces lactic acid. Aerobic respiration is the more efficient process and is the main form of respiration when oxygen is available.

items.meaning: Respiration with oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water and energy.
Respiration without oxygen, producing less energy and products such as alcohol and carbon dioxide in plants and yeast.
Anaerobic breakdown of glucose to ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide, as in yeast.
A substance, such as glucose, that is broken down in respiration to release energy.

items.text: Yeast in sugary dough produces carbon dioxide, which helps the dough rise; this is an example of anaerobic respiration in action.
items.note: The same process is used in making bread and alcoholic drinks.

items.text: Water plants kept in sunlight may give off bubbles of oxygen from photosynthesis, but they also respire all the time.
items.note: The two processes can hide each other if only one is observed.

learn.title: Where and how respiration occurs in plants

blocks.text: Respiration occurs in the cells of all parts of a plant — roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits — not only in the green parts. In each cell, glucose and other foods are broken down in a series of steps. The first steps occur in the cytoplasm, and the later steps occur in the mitochondria if oxygen is present. Oxygen used in respiration comes from the air spaces inside the plant; in leaves it can enter through the stomata and in other parts through bark openings or other surfaces. Carbon dioxide produced in respiration is released in the same way. Because respiration is happening constantly, plants need a continuous supply of food and oxygen, even when they are not photosynthesising.

items: All living plant cells respire, not only green cells.
Respiration happens day and night.
Oxygen enters the plant through air spaces, stomata and other surfaces.
Carbon dioxide produced in respiration is released from the plant.
Energy from respiration is used for growth, transport, absorption and other life activities.
Respiration and photosynthesis are separate processes, though they may happen together in green cells.

items.text: A germinating root tip respires actively even though it is not green and does not photosynthesise.
items.note: This shows respiration is a general cell process, not a green-leaf process only.

items.text: A developing fruit respires to supply energy for its growth and ripening changes.
items.note: Respiration supports development in non-leaf organs too.

blocks.text: The fact that plants respire can be shown by experiments. A common example is to use a small organism or germinating seeds in a closed vessel with lime water or with a chemical that shows the presence of carbon dioxide. If respiration occurs, carbon dioxide is produced and can be detected. Another common class of experiments is to compare a living, growing preparation with a dead or dry control, so that the change can be linked to life and respiration rather than to decay or to an outside source. The essential idea is that respiration produces carbon dioxide and uses oxygen, so evidence for one of these changes is evidence for respiration. The experiments must also control for photosynthesis, which can use carbon dioxide, because otherwise the result may be misleading.

items.meaning: Calcium hydroxide solution that turns milky in the presence of carbon dioxide.
A comparison preparation kept under similar conditions except for the factor being tested.
Gas produced in respiration and also used in photosynthesis.

items: Respiration in plants can be shown by the production of carbon dioxide.

items.text: Germinating seeds in a closed jar over lime water can show carbon dioxide production and hence respiration.

items.text: A comparison between a living plant part and a boiled or dead one can show that the gas comes from respiration, not from something else.

assessment.title: Respiration in Plants: check your understanding
instructions: Answer the short questions in one or two sentences each.
For the long and analytical questions, write in full sentences and name the processes, products and conditions clearly.
All questions are original practice; they are not past paper questions.

exercises.answer: Respiration is the breakdown of food in living cells with the release of energy.
exercises.explanation: The definition should include food breakdown, living cells and energy release.

exercises.prompt: Give one difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
exercises.answer: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and produces more energy, while anaerobic respiration does not use oxygen and produces less energy.
exercises.explanation: Any clear difference, especially oxygen requirement or energy released, carries the marks.

exercises.prompt: State the products of aerobic respiration in plants.
exercises.answer: The products of aerobic respiration are carbon dioxide, water and energy.
exercises.explanation: The three products should be named.

exercises.prompt: Why is respiration not the same as photosynthesis?
exercises.answer: Photosynthesis makes food using light energy, carbon dioxide and water, and releases oxygen. Respiration breaks down food to release energy, uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. They are opposite in many respects and can happen at the same time in green cells.
exercises.explanation: The answer should contrast making food with releasing energy from food.

exercises.prompt: Describe a simple experiment to show that germinating seeds respire.
exercises.answer: Place germinating seeds in a sealed flask with a test tube of lime water. After some time the lime water turns milky because the seeds produce carbon dioxide during respiration. A control with dead or dry seeds should also be kept so that the change can be attributed to living respiration rather than to something else.
exercises.explanation: The answer should mention germinating seeds, carbon dioxide and a control for comparison.

exercises.prompt: Why do plants need respiration even when they are photosynthesising?
exercises.answer: Plants need respiration because energy is required for life processes such as growth, transport, absorption and repair, and photosynthesis does not supply energy directly for these activities. Respiration releases this energy from food in every living cell, also at night when photosynthesis is not occurring.
exercises.explanation: The answer should link energy need to life processes and note that respiration is continuous.

questions.prompt: Respiration is the process by which cells:
questions.explanation: Respiration is the breakdown of food in living cells with the release of energy.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 'make food' — that describes photosynthesis, not respiration.

questions.prompt: Which gas is produced in aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide, water and energy.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing oxygen — oxygen is used in aerobic respiration, not produced.

questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing anaerobic respiration — that is the less efficient process.

questions.prompt: In plants and yeast, anaerobic respiration may produce:
questions.explanation: In plants and yeast, anaerobic respiration commonly produces ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing lactic acid only — that is typical of animal muscle cells under oxygen shortage.

options: In all living cells, day and night
questions.answer: In all living cells, day and night
questions.explanation: All living plant cells respire, at all times, not only in green parts or only during the day.
questions.commonMistake: Saying 'only during the day' — respiration is continuous.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign that carbon dioxide is present?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky, which is a common test in respiration experiments.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing a colour change that is not associated with carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: respiration is the breakdown of food in living cells with the release of ________.
questions.explanation: The key result of respiration is the release of energy from food.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'oxygen' — oxygen is used in aerobic respiration, not the result released from food breakdown.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blanks: the common equation for aerobic respiration is glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + ________.
questions.explanation: Energy is the important product of aerobic respiration alongside carbon dioxide and water.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'oxygen' — oxygen is on the left side of the equation, not the product released.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, while anaerobic respiration does not. Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water, while anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast commonly produces alcohol and carbon dioxide. Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.
questions.explanation: Any two clear differences, such as oxygen need, products or energy released, carry the marks.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one difference or repeating the same point in two ways.

questions.prompt: Why do plants need respiration if they also photosynthesise?
questions.answer: Plants need respiration because photosynthesis makes food but does not directly supply the energy needed for life processes. Respiration releases energy from food for growth, transport, absorption, repair and other activities. It also happens at night when photosynthesis is not occurring, so the plant still needs energy.
questions.explanation: The answer should contrast making food with releasing energy and note that respiration is continuous.
questions.commonMistake: Saying plants respire only when they cannot photosynthesise — they respire all the time.

questions.prompt: Describe aerobic respiration in plants and state its importance.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of food, usually glucose, in the presence of oxygen. It occurs in the cytoplasm and mitochondria of living plant cells and produces carbon dioxide, water and energy. The energy released is used for life processes such as growth, absorption, transport and repair. Aerobic respiration is more efficient than anaerobic respiration because it completely breaks down glucose and releases more energy. It happens in all living plant cells day and night, not only in the green parts, and it continues even when photosynthesis is not occurring.
questions.explanation: A full answer should cover oxygen use, products, energy use, efficiency and where and when it occurs.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only the equation without explaining where or why it matters.

questions.prompt: A student sets up two flasks: one with germinating seeds and one with dry seeds, each with lime water. Only the flask with germinating seeds turns milky. What does this show, and why is the second flask important?
questions.answer: The milky lime water in the first flask shows that the germinating seeds are producing carbon dioxide, which is evidence that they are respiring. The second flask with dry seeds is the control. It is important because it shows that the change in lime water is due to the living, growing seeds and not to something in the air, the seeds' coverings, or the apparatus itself. Without the control, the result would be less convincing.
questions.explanation: The answer should link the milky water to carbon dioxide and respiration, and explain the control's role.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning the milky water but not explaining the purpose of the dry-seed flask.
